item.title: Reimagining Food Innovation
item.description: Some of the most significant innovations surrounding food are not high-tech scientific advances but low-tech social practices and relations, such as new ways of cooperating and distributing responsibility. To fix our broken food systems, we must demand that the best of these practices receive respect and investment.

item.title: Gun Buybacks Work, But Not the Way We Thought
item.description: Some argue that gun buybacks are pointless unless they lower homicide rates. But new research into Mexico City’s gun-buyback program suggests that such measures can meaningfully reduce nonlethal injuries, which are more common than homicides, and can have serious psychological and other lasting health consequences.

item.title: The Future of the Global Disability Agenda
item.description: The once-reasonable assumption that integrating disabled people into the existing multilateral order would help them benefit from the results being delivered no longer holds. Achieving better outcomes requires learning from disability movements about how to put diversity, access, care, and participation at the center of the agenda.

item.title: Can the AI Mineral Rush Advance a Just Green Transition?
item.description: The scramble to secure huge amounts of copper, aluminum, lithium, cobalt, and other minerals for AI infrastructure risks undoing the progress made, as part of the green transition, toward more responsible mining practices. But it could also be an opportunity to support sustainable development in producer countries.

item.title: The Evolving Terrain of the Global AI Transformation
item.description: The race to build ever more powerful AI models is heating up, but so far there is little evidence of the promised productivity surge. Whether that changes will depend on how quickly employers adopt AI and whether governments can encourage its use while managing the risks of job losses and public backlash.

item.title: How Congress Can Give Americans What They Want
item.description: American households are footing the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran through higher prices and borrowing costs. Congress has the power to stop this by reclaiming its authority over tariff policy and the use of military force, and by requiring a public accounting of the costs of future wars.

item.title: The Revolt Against Oligarchy
item.description: The extraordinary power wielded by today’s billionaires is a threat to democracy and the planet. Encouragingly, people around the world, frustrated by a lack of affordability and worsening job prospects, are beginning to discover just how much political power they can wield.

item.title: Who Can Speak for Europe in Peace Talks with Russia?
item.description: The European Union's inability to find one person to represent it in such negotiations reflects a structural failure, not a shortage of skilled personnel. That is why the EU should step aside and delegate the selection of an envoy to the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.

item.title: The Fossil-Fuel Endgame Doesn’t Require a COP Consensus
item.description: Despite the failure of this year's United Nations climate talks, there is no doubt that phasing out fossil fuels is the right goal. The only question is whether a coalition of the willing can use policy to push markets toward a faster, fairer, and smoother transition than the traditional COP process can deliver.

item.title: Who Controls America’s AI Chokepoint?
item.description: The saga of Jensen Huang's ouster and sudden return as Nvidia's chief executive has exposed a paradox at the heart of American technological hegemony. While Nvidia's AI chips give the United States leverage over China, the geopolitical power that Nvidia makes possible gives it leverage over the US.

item.title: Where Development Cooperation Still Lives
item.description: By helping developing economies build the capacity and infrastructure trade requires, the World Trade Organization's Aid for Trade initiative has contributed to a significant increase in these countries' share of global exports over the past 20 years. But the trade landscape is changing fast, and Aid for Trade must adapt.

item.title: Nvidia’s Liability Problem Isn’t Going Away
item.description: Given previous suspicions about Nvidia's engagement with China, one wonders if Jensen Huang’s admitted extramarital affairs are just a cover-up for more consequential violations and misrepresentations. Whatever the case, the problem is not limited to Huang; with his reinstatement as CEO, it involves the company's entire board.

item.title: Mapping Strategic Supply-Chain Risk
item.description: If there is a premium to be paid for resilient supply chains, who will foot the bill? The answer can be found through a three-stage approach of identifying current vulnerabilities, letting markets and public tenders price them, and then having national-security authorities intervene only where market pricing fails.

item.title: Holiday 2026 Reading List
item.description: In the bi-weekly PS Book Recommendations newsletter—available for free to all registered PS readers—we highlight insightful, informative, or otherwise compelling books, written or recommended by PS contributors. Here, we present a selection of recent works by PS contributors that are worth adding to your holiday shopping list (and your bookshelf).

item.title: The Summit of Self-Promotion
item.description: Despite claiming that world history was made in Shenzhen with the US–Russia–China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, the trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin was about optics, not substance. One of the many important problems they failed to address was China’s export-led growth.

item.title: Why Nvidia Couldn’t Quit Jensen Huang
item.description: Developing AI requires tremendous coordination across firms and sectors, from the AI labs themselves to energy and computing infrastructure, as well as long-term vision and patience. Whereas much of this coordination and planning is led by the government in China, in the US, it has been driven largely by one CEO.

item.title: Chips Too Big to Fail
item.description: The Trump administration pushed for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia to keep the stock market high, to feed a possible productivity surge, and to advance a US foreign policy built on reconciliation with China. But will Americans continue to believe in the AI miracle and this new version of Chimerica?

item.title: Amplifying the Voice of Human Limits
item.description: Tech leaders like Elon Musk have embraced Prometheus as a symbol of creation, conquest, and discovery. But the Promethean impulse must be balanced by the “Orphic” tradition’s respect for and contemplation of nature’s mystery.

item.title: Making the Most of South Korea’s Semiconductor Boom
item.description: The AI boom has driven South Korea’s economic growth well above expectations, thanks to soaring demand for advanced semiconductors. But AI’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment frenzy will continue, leaving the economy vulnerable to a downturn.

item.title: Is a Financial-Market Reckoning Imminent?
item.description: After a year of unprecedented AI investment, increasingly financed by debt in opaque private markets, growing unease about the industry’s future is reflected in sharp declines in the NASDAQ index and the S&P 500. But the stock market’s dependence on a handful of highly leveraged companies—and even a single CEO—is hardly the only source of global financial risk. Amid mounting fears, we asked PS contributors what to expect from financial markets in the year ahead.
